title: Qortex Systems - Hosted vs Private Latency & Throughput Interview
summary: Initial technical discovery to map Qortex latency/p95 and throughput requirements, evaluate hosted vs private deployment tradeoffs, and scope a short benchmark pilot. Primary concerns: p95 <= 250ms for short streaming responses, burst concurrency ~800 sessions, data residency and KMS, and cost vs latency trade-offs.
topics: p95 targets for streaming and non-streaming
hosted vs private (VPC) network hop and egress concerns
KV cache/prefix caching and batching strategies
security: SOC2, KMS, SSO, audit logs

Jai - share benchmark harness, sample runner, and S3 with test prompts by 2026-06-22

Schedule 2-hour pilot kickoff to run baseline p95 streaming tests (target week of 2026-06-29)

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-18
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Robin Ellis (Redwood AE), Jai Mathur (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Qortex CTO), Luis Ortega (Head of Platform), Priya Nair (SRE), Samir Patel (Product)

Summary (auto): Short discovery to align on latency SLOs and pilot scope.

[00:00] Robin: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Robin from Redwood Inference, AE on this account, and with me is Jai our systems SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Maya: Doing well, thanks. We wanted to dig into latency and throughput, particularly for streaming chat endpoints. We've got a hard p95 target for some flows.
[00:15] Robin: Great, yeah that's exactly what we wanted to go over. Jai, do you want to kick off with our typical questions?
[00:20] Jai: Sure. Quick one: what p95 are you trying to hold for user-visible streaming responses, and what are the typical token sizes?
[00:28] Luis: For our primary use-case, short answers, around 30-80 tokens per response, p95 ideally under 250ms end-to-end for the streaming appearance. For long form we accept 800-1200ms.
[00:40] Samir: To add, we have bursts during peak product launches — roughly 500 concurrent active chats sustained for 10-20 minutes and spikes to around 900-1,000 for 2-3 minutes.
[00:52] Jai: Okay, that helps. Are you currently hosting models on-prem, cloud, or using a third-party API?
[00:58] Maya: Right now we proxy to a managed API but latency is inconsistent; we're evaluating moving to a private deployment in our VPC or using Redwood dedicated.
[01:06] Priya: Security is non-negotiable — KMS for keys, audit logs, and our SSO federation. Also need data residency in eu-west-1 for some customers.
[01:16] Robin: Totally reasonable. We support KMS integrations and provide audit logs, and private deployments can run in your VPC for egress control.
[01:24] Jai: A few follow-ups: what's your acceptable cold-start behavior? Do you expect always-hot sessions or can you tolerate some warmup?
[01:32] Luis: We want steady-state near-perfect during business hours; cold-starts okay on edge cases but can't be 5-10s. We also want predictable token/sec throughput so downstream UI remains snappy.
[01:43] Jai: Got it. For streaming p95 250ms, usually hosted can meet that for short tokens depending on region and network hops; private in-VPC can shave off 30-80ms depending on your topology. But there are trade-offs on ops.
[01:57] Maya: Can you quantify the network hop? If we run in our VPC, what's typical additional latency vs hosted in the same region?
[02:05] Jai: Good question. If you run Redwood Private inside your VPC (we deploy control plane optionally out-of-band), the data path stays internal so you eliminate internet egress. That typically reduces median latency by ~20-40ms and p95 by 30-90ms for short sequences — depends on your load balancer + NAT gateway. For Hosted, we maintain regional endpoints; public internet adds variability.
[02:30] Speaker 3: Is the 30-90 ms figure for single-token generation or end-to-end streaming?
[02:33] Jai: It's end-to-end for a streaming chunk to first byte in a typical setup. For models with larger KV caches and longer past context, compute dominates so network impact shrinks.
[02:44] Maya: What about concurrency? If we hit 1k concurrent streams, how does Redwood handle constant batching?
[02:50] Jai: Our runtime uses continuous batching and auto-batching heuristics. For streaming we batch where possible but we prioritize latency SLOs per-request. On Dedicated pools you can reserve more capacity and we can provision worker count to keep tail latency down. We also have intelligent routing to fall back to smaller model variants if overloaded.
[03:08] Luis: Do you support quantized weights? We are exploring q4 and q8xx variants to save GPU memory.
[03:13] Jai: Yes — our runtime supports multiple quantization profiles; we can recommend quantization vs latency trade-offs for your workload. Typically quantization reduces memory and allows more concurrent sessions per GPU but you may see a small p95 regression depending on the model. We'll put numbers in the pilot.
[03:29] Robin: Quick question to understand your cost constraint — are you optimizing for lowest unit cost or strict latency?
[03:34] Samir: Latency first for the main product path, cost second. But we still need predictable OPEX.
[03:40] Jai: Alright. For the pilot we'll target a baseline: hosted in eu-west-1 with a small dedicated pool vs a private VPC deployment to show delta. We'll run token/sec benchmarks and streaming p95 tests.
[03:51] Maya: On token/sec, what tooling do you use? We want reproducible numbers.
[03:55] Jai: We use a benchmark harness that does deterministic sequences, simulates streaming chunk sizes, measures first-byte latency and p95 for end-to-end. We'll share the harness and a sample load file.
[04:06] Priya: We'll need to run this behind our firewall — can we run the harness from our infra?
[04:10] Jai: Yes, we'll provide a containerized harness. You can run it from your internal infra against a private deployment or our hosted endpoint.
[04:18] Luis: How do you handle KV cache and prefix caching? We have a lot of repeated context across sessions.
[04:23] Jai: We support prefix caching and KV cache reuse. In our serving runtime the KV cache is re-used across sessions where appropriate; it cuts token compute substantially for repeating contexts. We'll advise cache TTLs and sharding strategy during the pilot.
[04:36] Maya: Network details: we need to know port egress, IPs, and typical bandwidth per session.
[04:41] Robin: We'll include a network appendix with ports, IP ranges, and recommended NAT configuration. Bandwidth per streaming session is small — the main cost is CPU/GPU compute per token.
[04:51] [05:00] (classifier mislabel) Speaker 5: A quick nit — how deterministic are p95 numbers across days? We've seen swings due to noisy neighbors.
[05:07] Jai: On Hosted we enforce isolation via scheduling and rate limits; Dedicated gives you reserved capacity which smooths p95. Private gives you full control but adds ops. For noisy neighbors we recommend dedicated or private.
[05:18] Maya: For the pilot, can we run a scenario: base load 500 concurrent streams steady for 20 minutes, then a 3-minute spike to 1,000, and measure p95 and token/sec?
[05:28] Robin: Yes, that maps exactly to the kind of tests we run. We'll propose a config in the test plan.
[05:33] Priya: Any gotchas around TLS termination and cert management in private?
[05:38] Jai: We can integrate with your cert manager and also support passing through TLS to your LB; for private we can integrate with your KMS/HSM for key ops.
[05:46] Luis: About OCSP and audit logs — we need full request-level traces for compliance.
[05:50] Robin: We capture per-request traces and can export logs to your SIEM or S3 with redaction options. We'll include retention policies and compliance docs.
[06:00] Samir: Will you support A/B canary rollouts between model variants? We plan to test faster but cheaper models to control cost.
[06:06] Jai: Yes, rollouts and traffic split are built into the control plane. You can set percent-based routing, automatic rollback on error or latency regressions.
[06:15] Maya: Back to numbers — do you have example p95s for a 7B and 13B open model on a single GPU in eu-west? Ballpark is fine.
[06:23] Jai: Ballpark: for 7B generation of short 40-token responses, streaming first-byte p95 on a well sized node can be 80-180ms depending on batching. For 13B it's more like 130-300ms. That assumes optimized kernels and a GPU with NVLink. We'll provide exacts in the pilot.
[06:42] Maya: Those numbers are helpful. We also care about cold-start and scaling behavior — if an instance gets evicted, how long to spin up replacement?
[06:50] Jai: For Dedicated we keep a buffer of warm workers to avoid long cold starts. Private behavior depends on your autoscaler; ours recommends a pool policy with warm standbys. Cold start could be seconds to tens of seconds if model needs to reload weights.
[07:04] Luis: For our UI we send many small prompts per session; can batching introduce latency spikes because requests are held to fill batch?
[07:11] Jai: We use latency-aware batching. If batching windows would violate per-request SLO we bypass and serve immediately, so you shouldn't see hold-for-batch delays for your primary flows. Batching benefits throughput overall but we tune to SLOs.
[07:24] Maya: Any limits on token/sec per session?
[07:27] Jai: No hard limits; throughput is bounded by model throughput on the worker. For streaming we expose token/sec metrics; for tight workloads we can recommend sharding across workers or pinned capacity.
[07:36] Priya: On instrumentation, can we get per-token latency breakdowns (kernel, memcpy, serialization, network)?
[07:42] Robin: We provide token-level traces and pipeline breakdowns in the console and can surface custom traces via tracing hooks.
[07:50] [08:00] (audio noise) Speaker 2: Sorry, there's a little background —
[08:03] Samir: No worries. One more: in private deployment, what's the upgrade path? We run quarterly maintenance windows.
[08:09] Jai: Upgrades can be rolled with canary and drain; private deploys follow a maintenance schedule you control. We'll help with automation.
[08:17] Maya: For the pilot, what success criteria should we agree to?
[08:21] Robin: How about three metrics: p95 streaming first-byte under 250ms for short flows, steady-state throughput sustaining 500 concurrent streams with p95 under 350ms, and reproducible token/sec numbers within 10% across runs.
[08:33] Maya: Sounds good. Samir: Also include stability during the 3-minute spike — p95 shouldn't double.
[08:39] Robin: Agreed. We'll codify that in the test plan.
[08:43] Jai: I'll put together the test matrix: models (7B/13B), quantization (fp16, q4), hosting modes (hosted/dedicated/private), scenarios (steady 500, spike to 1k), and metrics (first-byte p95, end-to-end p95, token/sec, CPU/GPU utilization).
[08:58] Priya: For private networking we'll need an ops runbook.
[09:01] Robin: We'll include runbook and network appendix.
[09:05] Maya: Any estimate on how long the pilot takes? We want minimal disruption.
[09:09] Jai: Setup ~3 business days for hosted/dedicated config, private will need coordination with your networking and could be 1-2 weeks depending on approvals. Running the baseline tests will take a day or two.
[09:19] Luis: Cost estimate ballpark? We need to budget.
[09:21] Robin: We'll include a rough cost per-million tokens for hosted and a reserved-monthly estimate for dedicated. Private is variable with infra. We'll send a short cost sheet.
[09:30] Maya: Great. Any final questions?
[09:33] Samir: Do you have a public incident history or SLOs we can review?
[09:36] Robin: Yes, SOC2 and SLO docs attached in the materials we'll send.
[09:40] Priya: Ok that's all from our side.
[09:43] Robin: Awesome. Recap of next steps: Robin sends pricing and SOC2, Jai shares harness and test plan, Priya shares firewall info and prompt sets. We'll target pilot the week of 06/29.
[09:57] End meeting.
